info.name: E-Commerce Microservices
info.description:
A plain collection for driving the API by hand: one folder per resource, no assertions.

Run the folders **top to bottom on a fresh start** — Auth saves a token, Catalogue saves a product id, and the later folders use them.

Select the `ecommerce · local` environment before running anything.

The assertion-heavy version, with the deliberately-failing requests and the cache and rate-limit checks, was removed on purpose while the order workflow is being built. It is in git history if it is wanted back.

exec: // Runs before every request in the collection.
'Select the "ecommerce · local" environment in the top-right picker.'

variable.value: All real values live in the environment, not here, so the collection can be shared without carrying anyone's tokens.

item.name: 1 · Auth
item.description: Register saves the token every other folder uses. Register generates a fresh email each run, so it can be re-run any number of times.

request.description: A fresh email per run, so the unique index never turns this into a 409.
200, not 201 — logging in creates nothing.
The profile behind the current token.

item.name: 2 · Catalogue
item.description: Category → product → publish → read. The product created here is what the Inventory, Cart and Orders folders use.

request.description: Slug and name are both uniquely indexed, so both are generated per run.
Note the response: `price` comes back as the string "1899.00", and `status` is DRAFT. Nothing goes on sale by accident.
Required before the Cart folder: a DRAFT product cannot be added to a cart.
A partial update: send only what changes. With RabbitMQ running this also publishes `product.price_changed`.

item.name: 3 · Inventory
item.description: Stock is three numbers: `onHand`, `reserved`, and `available` — which is derived, never stored. Run this after the Catalogue folder.

request.description: Opens at zero. Nothing arrives by magic.
Goods arrived: `onHand` goes up.
Promised to an order. `onHand` is unchanged — the goods are still in the warehouse — but `available` drops.
The promise is cancelled. This is the undo for a reservation.
Shipped: BOTH `onHand` and `reserved` go down.
A signed correction with a mandatory reason. An unexplained adjustment is indistinguishable from theft.
Every movement, append-only. The balance without this history could not be audited.

item.name: 4 · Cart
item.description: Always *your* cart — there is no `:cartId` in any route, so there is no id to tamper with. Needs a token from folder 1 and an ACTIVE product from folder 2.

request.description: An empty cart, not a 404. Calling it repeatedly yields the same one.
Note what the response contains that the request did not: `name` and `unitPrice`. Both are snapshotted by the server from the catalogue.
An upsert: quantity 3 on one line, not a second line.
PATCH sets the quantity; it is not a delta.
Empties it and KEEPS it — the row carries the identity abandonment analytics rely on.

item.name: 5 · Orders
item.description:
Milestone 8. `POST /orders` reads your cart, copies the lines into an order in one local transaction, returns it CONFIRMED, and publishes `order.confirmed`.

The Cart Service consumes that event and marks the cart CONVERTED — so the cart empties itself **a moment later**, not instantly. Needs RabbitMQ running.

One gap is still open and marked below: no stock is reserved at checkout.

request.description: So there is something to order.
An EMPTY body. The lines come from the cart and the owner from the verified token — a client that could name its own prices would order a laptop for a penny.
Yours only, newest first, in a paginated envelope.

item.name: The cart converted itself (give it a second)

request.description:
A NEW empty cart: the old one was marked CONVERTED by the `order.confirmed` event, and `GET /cart` creates a fresh one.

**This is not instant.** The Order Service published the event after its commit; RabbitMQ delivered it; the Cart Service handled it. If you still see the old cart, wait a second and re-send — or check that RabbitMQ is running. That gap is what eventual consistency means in practice.

item.name: ⚠ Stock did not move — still open

request.description:
`reserved` is unchanged: nothing calls the Inventory Service at checkout, so two customers can both order the last unit.

Fixing it means reserving stock per line — a write into another service’s database, which then needs an undo if a later step fails. That compensating workflow is deliberately not built; it is in the deferred table in `docs/PROJECT-PLAN.md` with the trigger that should bring it back.
A status change, and an `order.cancelled` event. Nothing was reserved and nobody was charged, so there is nothing to undo — the event is published only after the UPDATE actually matched a row.

item.name: 6 · Payments
item.description:
Milestone 9. Paying is a **separate call** from checkout, so each is retryable on its own.

`POST /payments` sends an `orderId` and a `paymentMethodToken` — never a card number, never an amount. The amount is read from the order server-side; the card was tokenised by the provider before it ever reached us.

The tokens force an outcome, the way every provider test card does:

| Token | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| `tok_ok` | approved |
| `tok_declined` | declined — insufficient funds |
| `tok_fraud` | declined — suspected fraud |
| `tok_timeout` | no answer at all (takes ~10s) |
| `tok_unavailable` | provider is down |
| `tok_flaky` | fails about half the time |

Two protections against a double charge, and they answer different questions:

| | Order index | Idempotency key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asks | does this order already have a payment? | have I seen this request before? |
| Answers | **409**, nothing charged | **the original response**, replayed |

Run folder `5 · Orders` first — this one pays for the order it left behind.

item.name: Place an order to pay for

request.description: Folder 5 cancels its order at the end, so this makes a fresh CONFIRMED one. Add something to the cart first if it is empty.

exec: // One key per attempt, reused by the next request to prove that a
// retry returns the SAME payment rather than making another.

request.description:
201. Note what comes back: a `reference` you could read down a phone, the provider own `providerReference`, a last-4 and a brand — and **not** the token or the key you sent. Anything echoed back ends up in a log.

The `Idempotency-Key` is generated per run by the pre-request script. A real client generates one per checkout attempt and reuses it across retries.

item.name: Send it again with the SAME key — 200, replayed

request.description:
**200, not 201** — nothing was created. The `Idempotent-Replay: true` header says so, and the body is the SAME payment: same id, same reference, same provider reference.

This is what a client that timed out actually needs. A 409 would tell it the order is covered; only the key tells it *what happened to its own request*.

item.name: The order is now PAID (give it a second)

request.description: `payment.succeeded` travelled over RabbitMQ and the Order Service moved the order CONFIRMED to PAID itself. Not instant — if it still says CONFIRMED, re-send. No service writes another service database.
Yours only, newest first — including the failures. One row per ATTEMPT, which is what support needs when a customer phones about a card that was refused.

The Payment Service reads the order first and finds it is no longer awaiting payment. This is the check that catches a stale checkout page — but note it is a *check*, not a constraint, and the last request in this folder shows why that matters.

item.name: Place another order (for the failure cases)

request.description: Add items to the cart first if it is empty — folder 4, or the first request of folder 5.

**402 Payment Required**, and `retryable: false`.

Not 400 — the request was perfectly well formed. Not 500 — nothing broke. Not 503 — sending it again produces the same refusal, and each attempt is a line on the customer statement.

The attempt is still recorded, with the provider reference, because that is what support quotes on the phone.

**503**, and `retryable: true`. We never got an answer, so the outcome is UNKNOWN — the charge may be settling right now. The row is FAILED with a NULL `providerReference`, which is exactly the case where you most want one.

The provider takes 30 seconds; the deadline is 10. Watch the clock in Postman — this is the failure that makes idempotency keys necessary, because a client that times out does not know whether it was charged.

item.name: A card number is refused at the edge — 400

request.description: `forbidNonWhitelisted` rejects it at the gateway, one hop before it could reach a log. A field that is silently ignored is a field somebody will eventually assume is being used.

item.name: Pay the same order with a NEW key — 409, nothing charged

request.description:
A different request, so the key does not match and there is nothing to replay. The **order index** refuses it instead — at INSERT, before the provider is called.

Read the message: *nothing was charged*. That is the difference between a constraint and a check: the constraint fires while refusing is still free.

item.name: Retry a declined card with a NEW key

request.description:
The declined attempt above left the order payable — a decline is not the end of an order, it is the commonest reason to reach for another card.

A NEW key, because a key identifies one ATTEMPT: reusing the old one would replay the 402 forever. Set `orderId2` to the order you declined, or just re-run the two requests above.

item.name: 7 · Notifications
item.description:
Milestone 10, pass 1. Every step of the earlier folders quietly sent an email; this folder is where you see them.

| Event | Email |
| --- | --- |
| `user.registered` | welcome |
| `order.confirmed` | order confirmation |
| `payment.succeeded` | payment receipt |

Nothing asked for those. The Notification Service listens to facts and decides for itself what they imply — which is why there is no `POST /notifications`.

**By default nothing is actually sent.** `MAIL_TRANSPORT=log` prints the subject and recipient to the service log. To see real messages, start MailHog, set `MAIL_TRANSPORT=smtp` in `.env`, restart, and read them at http://localhost:8025:

```bash
docker run -d --name ecommerce-mailhog -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 mailhog/mailhog
```

**Run folders 1 → 6 first.** The welcome email needs a registration that happened while this service was running, so re-run folder 1 if the stack was started after you registered.

exec: // Handy for the next request: how many the service thinks it has sent.

request.description:
Newest first. After folders 1 → 6 you should see a WELCOME, one or more ORDER_CONFIRMED, and a PAYMENT_RECEIPT.

Each row records the address it went TO — not the contact’s current address — for the same reason a cart line snapshots a price: where it went is a fact.
The type is named after the BUSINESS EVENT, not after the template — `PAYMENT_RECEIPT`, not `receipt-email-v2`. Naming these after templates means a redesign becomes a contract change.

Usually empty with `MAIL_TRANSPORT=log`.

Two ways to make it non-empty, both worth doing once:

1. Set `MAIL_TRANSPORT=smtp` **without** starting MailHog. The send fails, the row is recorded FAILED with `ECONNREFUSED`, and nothing throws — because throwing out of a message handler would make RabbitMQ redeliver and retry a broken address forever.

2. Place an order as a user who registered **before** the Notification Service was ever started. It has no contact row for them, so it records a FAILED notification saying exactly that instead of silently skipping it.

item.name: Place another order — watch the email follow

request.description:
Add something to the cart first if it is empty (folder 4). Then re-run the first request in this folder: a new ORDER_CONFIRMED appears a moment later.

Watch the Cart Service log at the same time. **Both** services received this one event, each with its own copy — the cart converted itself and the notification service emailed. On the single shared queue this project used until M10, they would have taken turns.

Note also what each did with a redelivery. The cart is safe for free (`WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'`); the notification service had to claim the event id to be safe at all.

item.name: One confirmation per order, however many deliveries

request.description:
**The thing to try.**

RabbitMQ delivers at-least-once, so this handler will eventually be given the same message twice. Force it: open the management UI at :15672, find `notification_service`, and use **Get messages** with *Requeue: yes* — or stop the service mid-handler and start it again.

The count here does not change. The service claimed the `eventId` in a `processed_events` ledger before it sent anything, and the second delivery finds the claim taken. Its log says so at debug level: *already handled, skipping*.

Every other consumer in this system survives a redelivery for free, by being naturally repeatable — `UPDATE carts SET status='CONVERTED' WHERE status='ACTIVE'` does nothing the second time. **There is no WHERE clause that un-sends an email**, which is why this is the only service in the project with a ledger.

Claiming BEFORE the send is a deliberate trade: a crash in between costs one missed email, where claiming afterwards would cost a duplicate on every crash.

item.name: 8 · Cleanup
item.description: Run last, or not at all. Deleting the product makes the Inventory, Cart and Orders folders fail until the Catalogue folder is run again.

request.description: Soft delete: the row stays and `deleted_at` is set, so orders that reference this product still make sense. Kept in its own folder because deleting the product breaks every folder above it.
